turns.text: Hi Wren, hi Mr. Okafor. Thanks for coming in. Mr. Okafor, your log is very easy to read, I appreciate the bullet points. Wren, I'd like to go through the last two weeks and then make a plan for the next step. Sound okay?
Sure.
So the orthodontist is the big one. Sixth floor. The first time, you got in, and then jumped back out as the doors were closing. Can you tell me what was happening right then?
It's kind of stupid. I got in and I was fine, and then the doors started closing and I just thought, what if it stops between floors. And I couldn't think about anything else. So I got out.
It's not stupid. That's a really clear description. When the doors started closing, the thought showed up, what if it gets stuck. And then what? If it got stuck, what would happen next?
I'd be stuck in a box. And it gets hot and there's no air, and I wouldn't be able to breathe. And nobody would come for like hours.
So the scary part is being stuck and not being able to breathe. Thank you. Has that ever happened to you, or someone you know?
No. Dad asked me that too. I just saw a video once.
She saw a clip online, some people stuck in an elevator in an office building. That was in the summer. It started after that, I think.
That makes sense. On the thermometer, zero to ten, riding up to the sixth floor at the orthodontist. Where are you?
Eight. Maybe seven now, since I did it once.
Let's talk about that, because last Tuesday you actually rode it. That's a big deal. Mr. Okafor, you wrote that she stood at the panel and held the door-open button.
Every floor. So the doors would open on two, three, four, five, nobody there. It took forever. But she did it.
Wren, what was holding the button doing for you?
If the doors open I can get out. If it's going to get stuck I can just get out at the next floor.

So the button is like an escape hatch. It makes sense you'd want one. The problem is, every time you ride with the escape hatch, your brain gives the credit to the button. It thinks, I was safe because I could get out. It doesn't learn, I was safe because elevators almost never get stuck. So the next step is going to be riding without holding the button. Not today, and not at the sixth floor first.
Okay. That sounds hard.
It should sound a bit hard. Now, your aunt's building. Mr. Okafor, that looks different from the orthodontist.

It's an older building, fourth floor. She rides it, but only if I'm in there with her. When we were leaving last week she waited by the door until I'd said goodbye to my sister, so we could go down together.
And you wrote that she counts the floors.
Under her breath. Lips moving. I didn't know if that was a thing or not.
Wren, what's the counting about?
I don't know. I count stuff a lot. Like stairs too. I don't think it's the elevator.
Okay, that's helpful. I'm not going to decide what it is yet. If you notice yourself counting other places, maybe jot it down. What number is your aunt's elevator, with Dad in it?
Like a six. It's old and it shakes. But Dad's in there.
Six with Dad. And without Dad?
I've never done that. I don't know. Higher.
There was also the car wash, that one time. She asked to get out and waited by the vacuums.
I saw that. Wren, is that the same worry, getting stuck?
Kind of. The doors lock and the brushes come. I just don't like it.

Okay. We'll put that on the list but we won't work on it this week. Let's build from where you are. Here's what I'm suggesting. The public library on your side of town has a small elevator, two floors. This week, step one: ride it with Dad, up and down, three times in a row, and you don't touch the panel at all. Dad presses the button. What number would that be?
With Dad, two floors, no button. Four, maybe.
Four. Then step two, same day if it goes okay: you ride one floor by yourself, and Dad takes the stairs and meets you. What number is that?
Six. Okay, that's scary, but it's one floor.

One floor. You don't have to love it. You just have to stay in until the doors open on their own. Mr. Okafor, there's a part for you too. I noticed you call ahead to the front desk when she takes the stairs.
Yeah, so they don't give away the slot.

I get it. For the next appointment, I'd like you to not plan around the stairs. Leave at the normal time. If she takes the stairs, that's okay, she can, but you don't walk with her and you don't call ahead. You take the elevator and meet her at the top. That's not to punish her, it's so the stairs stop being the easy plan.
That's fair. When's the next appointment, Wren, two weeks?
Three weeks. And if I do the library thing I might do the ortho one.

That would be up to you, and I'd love to hear about it. So, this week: library elevator with Dad, three rides, no touching the panel. Then one floor alone. Dad, you log the numbers she gives you. And at the next ortho visit, you take the elevator, and you don't walk the stairs with her or call ahead. Everyone okay with that?
Yep. Library, three rides, then one alone. I'll write it down.
Okay. Can it be Saturday?
Saturday is perfect. Great work today, Wren. See you both in a week.
